sentences.text: Rutiodon, meaning "wrinkle tooth," was an extinct genus of phytosaurs that lived during the Late Triassic in the eastern United States.
Although it resembled a crocodile, Rutiodon had nostrils positioned far back on the head near the eyes rather than at the snout tip.
The animal possessed enlarged front teeth and a narrow jaw similar to that of a modern gharial.
Its back, sides, and tail were covered with bony plates, similar to crocodiles.
The largest skull referred to Rutiodon measures 77.3 cm (30.4 inches) in length.
Rutiodon was one of the largest carnivores of its time, reaching lengths of up to 8 meters and weighing about 1 metric ton.
The holotype of R. manhattanensis possesses the largest femur ever observed in phytosaurs, measuring 43-44 cm (17 inches).

Rutiodon is one of the best-known phytosaurs and appeared in the 2001 Discovery Channel program When Dinosaurs Roamed America, where it was depicted unsuccessfully attacking a Coelophysis near a riverbank.
Rutiodon carolinensis was originally named by Ebenezer Emmons in 1856 based on fossils from the Deep River coal field in North Carolina.
A second species, R. manhattanensis, was discovered in 1910 near Fort Lee and named due to its proximity to Manhattan.
Friedrich von Huene described R. manhattanensis in 1913, naming it after its proximity to Manhattan.
A small partial phytosaur skull was discovered in 1963 at the Granton Quarry in North Bergen, New Jersey.
Fossils tentatively referred to R. carolinensis were unearthed in 1959 in Fairfax County, Virginia, near the construction site of Dulles International Airport.
Researchers suggest this carnivore likely caught fish and may have trapped terrestrial animals near the shores of water bodies.
Rutiodon is classified as an animal in the phylum Chordata, class Sauropsida, order Archosauria, and family Phytosauridae.
Rutiodon belongs to the clade Phytosauridae (Mystriosuchinae) and is outside the clade Leptosuchomorpha.
Recent studies place Rutiodon in the phytosaur family tree as more derived than Paleorhinus but less derived than Leptosuchus.
Rutiodon is classified within the family Parasuchidae.
Rutiodon is classified as a reptile.
R. manhattanensis is differentiated from R. carolinensis by having a proportionally larger tibia and a more robust hip.
Rutiodon lived from the Carnian to the Norian stages, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.

Fossils of Rutiodon carolinensis have been found in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Virginia, while the genus is known from the eastern United States, including North Carolina, New York, and New Jersey.
Some authors doubt the validity of R. manhattanensis, suggesting differences between the species may result from sexual dimorphism.
A 2001 abstract proposed that Rutiodon carolinensis was a synonym of Angistorhinus, suggesting Angistorhinus was ancestral to Rutiodon.
